lead: A serviceable aircraft, a healthy crew, and still it flies into a hill. That is controlled flight into terrain (CFIT), which has killed more people than any other cause in jet aviation. The cure is a warning that speaks before the ground arrives. Terrain awareness and ground proximity warning systems — GPWS, TAWS, EGPWS — compare the aircraft's path with the ground, first only the ground below, later a stored map of the terrain ahead, and call "pull up" early enough to climb away.
prereq: You need: the radar (radio) altimeter from 5.9, the glideslope of an ILS from 5.3, the GNSS position fix from 5.6, the position-error ideas of 5.7, and the barometric altimeter from Unit 3.

sections.h3: Why the ground kills: height above ground

blocks.text: Controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) is the accident in which an airworthy aircraft, flown by a qualified crew, is flown into ground, water or an obstacle the crew never saw in time. It happens at night, in cloud, over hilly ground, after a small altitude or track error.

Two heights exist in the cockpit. The barometric altimeter of Unit 3 shows height above a pressure datum and cannot know that a hill stands in the way. The radio altimeter times an echo and reads the height above the surface directly below, over roughly 0 to 2500 ft. That reading is radio altitude, RA.

Every reactive warning below is built from RA plus sink rate, airspeed, gear and flap position, and — in one mode only — the ILS glideslope. RA looks straight down, so the warning is late, typically 10 to 30 s before impact, and blind to a ridge 5 km ahead.

Classic GPWS is a set of seven modes. Each mode is an envelope: a limit that changes with RA, not a fixed number. Early units compared the envelope with barometric sink rate or the rate of change of RA; digital units added airspeed, gear, flap and ILS deviation.

blocks.text: Mode 1 works on barometric sink rate, gated by RA: a high sink rate is normal at 10 000 ft, so the allowed sink rate falls as RA falls. Crossing it gives the soft "SINK RATE"; a further crossing gives "PULL UP". Mode 2 has separate clean and flap-down envelopes, because an aircraft on final legitimately closes with the ground at 700 ft/min. Mode 3 guards the climb-out with gear still down. Mode 4 calls "TOO LOW GEAR" or "TOO LOW FLAPS" when the aircraft is low with the configuration wrong, then "TOO LOW TERRAIN".

Mode 5 is the only reactive mode that needs a ground aid: it is armed when an ILS is tuned and the aircraft sits more than about 1.3 dots below the beam at low RA. It says the aircraft is low on the approach, nothing about terrain. Mode 6 is a reminder; Mode 7 gives windshear warning from the airspeed and vertical-path signature.

sections.h3: TAWS: looking ahead with a database

blocks.text: A terrain awareness and warning system (TAWS), also sold as enhanced GPWS, keeps those seven modes and adds a forward look. It carries a digital terrain database — a grid of the highest elevation per cell plus known towers — a position from GNSS (5.6) or the flight management system, and a computer that projects the current track, speed and vertical path forward.

blocks.where: t is the time to impact in seconds; h is the height above the terrain ahead in ft; dh/dt is the closing (descent) rate in ft/s. Use climb rate in the same form to check whether the aircraft can still out-climb the slope.

blocks.text: Caution is amber, on the display and as a soft voice, about 60 s before predicted impact: "TERRAIN AHEAD". Warning is red with the hard command "TERRAIN, PULL UP" at about 30 s. Alert times vary with manufacturer, speed and phase of flight.

Inhibits exist because a warning that cries wolf gets switched off. Gear down silences some Mode 1 and Mode 4 alerts; a TERR INHIBIT switch lets the crew quiet nuisance alerts on a steep approach into a terrain-ringed airfield, flying the approach on the chart alone.

items: Database currency: a new tower, cable or building is invisible until the database is updated, and many wires and unlit obstacles are never mapped.
Position error: a GNSS outage leaving inertial-only position, a wrong datum, or a bad flight-management position puts the predicted path in the wrong place.
It warns; it does not fly. The escape is a maximum-performance climb the pilot must make.

figure.caption: The upper branch is the reactive GPWS, which measures the ground straight below with the radio altimeter. The lower branch adds a terrain database and a position to look forward along the flight path.

examples.question: An aircraft is at 1800 ft above ground level, descending at 1800 ft/min towards level terrain. TAWS look-ahead is set to alert 30 s before predicted impact. (a) Find the time to impact now. (b) When does the alert come, and at what height? (c) The altimeter sub-scale is set 5 hPa wrong — how much barometric height error does that add?
steps: (a) Time to impact = height ÷ descent rate = 1800 ft ÷ 1800 ft/min = 1.0 min = 60 s.
(b) 60 s is more than the 30 s threshold, so no alert yet. The alert comes after a further 30 s of descent.
Height then = 1800 ft × (30 s ÷ 60 s) = 900 ft above ground level.
(c) Near the surface 1 hPa ≈ 27 ft, so 5 hPa × 27 ft/hPa = 135 ft of barometric height error.
The reactive modes read radio altitude and are unaffected; the look-ahead path uses barometric height, so the 135 ft matters there.
examples.answer: Time to impact is 60 s, the alert comes 30 s later at 900 ft above ground level, and a 5 hPa sub-scale error is about 135 ft of barometric height error.
examples.check:
h = 1800.0
rate = 1800.0
t = h / rate * 60.0
print(t)
lead = 30.0
h_alert = h * lead / t
print(h_alert)
print(t - lead)
print(5 * 27)

traps: GPWS is reactive and looks down with the radio altimeter; TAWS look-ahead is predictive and needs a terrain database plus a position. Do not swap the two.
Mode 1 (sink rate) uses barometric descent rate gated by RA; Mode 5 (glideslope) needs a tuned ILS and is below-path deviation in dots. Not the same warning.
Quote radio altitude, not barometric altitude, as the gating quantity of Modes 1 to 5. A barometric height of 900 ft over high ground may be 300 ft above the hill.
Inhibits are normal. A landing configuration or an inhibit switch suppresses some alerts, so "no warning" does not mean "no risk".
Barometric sub-scale error: 1 hPa near the surface is about 27 ft, so 5 hPa is about 135 ft.

quiz.q: What does CFIT stand for, and what makes it different from an aircraft failure?
quiz.a: Controlled flight into terrain: an airworthy aircraft under control is flown into ground or an obstacle the crew did not see in time. Nothing has failed mechanically.

quiz.q: Which sensor feeds the reactive GPWS modes, and what quantity does it measure?
quiz.a: The radio (radar) altimeter. It measures height above the surface directly below the aircraft, from about 0 to 2500 ft, and that reading is the radio altitude RA.

quiz.q: Why does Mode 2 have separate flap-up and flap-down envelopes?
quiz.a: The warning compares the rate at which the ground is closing with a limit. On final approach with flap down, the aircraft closes with the ground at a few hundred ft/min by design, so a single clean-configuration limit would either be too sensitive on approach or too slack in the cruise. Two envelopes let the clean limit be tight and the landing limit loose.

quiz.q: Why is a barometric altimeter useless as the source for Mode 4?
quiz.a: The barometric altimeter measures height above a pressure datum, so its reading depends on the local pressure setting and carries no information about the hill or the ground below. Mode 4 needs true clearance above the surface, which only the radio altimeter gives.

quiz.q: An aircraft is at 2700 ft above ground level, descending at 900 ft/min over level terrain, with the look-ahead warning set at 30 s. Find the time to impact and the height at which the warning sounds.
quiz.a: Time to impact = 2700 ÷ 900 = 3 min = 180 s. The warning comes when 30 s remain, that is after 150 s of descent. Descent in that time = 900 × (150 ÷ 60) = 2250 ft, so the warning height is 2700 − 2250 = 450 ft above ground level.

quiz.q: An aircraft flies towards a newly built radio mast that is not in its terrain database. Why does neither the look-ahead nor the reactive GPWS give a timely warning?
quiz.a: Look-ahead compares the predicted path with stored terrain and obstacle elevations; an unmapped mast has no entry, so it predicts clear ground and stays silent. The reactive modes measure only the height of the surface directly below: a thin mast is a poor reflector and a brief RA change is not a clearance or sink-rate exceedance, so they too stay silent. Unmapped obstacles are the classic blind spot of both systems; only rising ground around the mast would eventually trigger a reactive alert, and then too late.

quiz.q: Why do crews inhibit some terrain alerts on steep approaches into airfields ringed by high ground?
quiz.a: The look-ahead projection assumes a normal climb-out and normal approach geometry. On a steep, curved approach the projected path meets terrain that the aircraft will in fact clear, so amber and red alerts fire repeatedly and would be ignored or disabled entirely. Inhibiting keeps the crew's trust in the system; the cost is that those alerts are gone for that approach.

quiz.q: The altimeter sub-scale is set 5 hPa too low. Estimate the barometric height error and say which TAWS functions it affects.
quiz.a: Near the surface 1 hPa ≈ 27 ft, so the error is 5 × 27 = 135 ft. It affects the barometric height used in the look-ahead path and in Mode 1's sink-rate comparison; it does not affect the radio-altimeter gating.

beyond: Not for the exam. Helicopter versions (HTAWS) use a smaller look-ahead volume and steeper climb assumptions, because a helicopter can stop rather than climb. Synthetic vision shows the same terrain database on a head-down display, and enhanced vision adds an infrared or millimetre-wave image so an unmapped obstacle becomes visible. Database currency is the weak link: a new tower is invisible until the next update. Search next for "helicopter TAWS" and "terrain database obstacle data standard".
